question: According to announcements by the Tunisian government, a negotiation process has been launched with the EU with the aim of increasing the existing duty-free export quota for Tunisian olive oil, which could reach up to 100 000 tonnes per year.

Meanwhile, according to Commission data, olive oil imports from Tunisia up to August 2025 amounted to 131 000 tonnes, an increase of 11 % compared to the 2023/24 trading year and 7.3 % compared to the five-year average. At the same time, the average import price of Tunisian olive oil decreased from EUR 5.48/kg in November 2024 to EUR 3.48/kg in August 2025.

These developments are causing concern among Greek olive producers, at a time when the sector is facing increased production costs, price pressure and intense competition, while also raising issues of transparency, traceability and fair competition in the single market. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the intention to increase the duty-free export quota for olive oil to the EU and what actions or assessments has it already carried out?

Does the Commission intend to carry out an assessment of the impact on the European olive oil market and producers in order to take measures to strengthen controls, transparency and equal treatment of imports from non-EU countries?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) On 29 January 2026 the Commission received an official communication from the Tunisian authorities requesting a revision of the Protocol on agriculture of the Association Agreement with Tunisia. However, the Commission does not envisage additional trade concessions for agricultural products originating in Tunisia including olive oil.

The Commission recognises the importance of a high level of protection of human health and the environment in the Vision for Agriculture and Food1. Food imported from third countries and food produced in the EU must comply with very strict sanitary requirements. The Commission committed to a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products and a strengthening of import controls2.

The Commission launched an impact assessment with a view to strengthening alignment of the EU’s production standards on most hazardous pesticides with requirements applicable to imported products3. Finally, a task force4 has recently been created to ensure imports meet EU standards, in particular on food and feed safety, pesticide residues and to coordinate monitoring of specific imported products.
